claim: Otolith organs in the inner ear and neuromasts in the fish lateral-line harbor two populations of hair cells oriented to detect stimuli in opposing directions.
source: Otolith organs in the inner ear and neuromasts in the fish lateral-line harbor two populations of hair cells oriented to detect stimuli in opposing directions.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The transcription factor EMX2 is regionally expressed in just one hair cell population and acts through the receptor GPR156 to reverse cell orientation relative to the other population.
source: The underlying mechanism is highly conserved: the transcription factor EMX2 is regionally expressed in just one hair cell population and acts through the receptor GPR156 to reverse cell orientation relative to the other population.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (Kindt et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2017) and represents established findings.

claim: In mouse and zebrafish, loss of Emx2 results in sensory organs that harbor only one hair cell orientation and are not innervated properly.
source: In mouse and zebrafish, loss of Emx2 results in sensory organs that harbor only one hair cell orientation and are not innervated properly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ji et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2017).

claim: In zebrafish, Emx2 confers hair cells with reduced mechanosensory properties.
source: In zebrafish, Emx2 also confers hair cells with reduced mechanosensory properties.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kindig et al., 2023.

claim: Otolith organs in Gpr156 mouse mutants have normal zonal organization.
source: We find that otolith organs in Gpr156 mouse mutants have normal zonal organization and normal type I-II hair cell distribution and mechano-electrical transduction properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Otolith organs in Gpr156 mouse mutants have normal type I-II hair cell distribution.
source: We find that otolith organs in Gpr156 mouse mutants have normal zonal organization and normal type I-II hair cell distribution and mechano-electrical transduction properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1D-I.

claim: Otolith organs in Gpr156 mouse mutants have normal mechano-electrical transduction properties.
source: We find that otolith organs in Gpr156 mouse mutants have normal zonal organization and normal type I-II hair cell distribution and mechano-electrical transduction properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 2-4.

claim: gpr156 zebrafish mutants lack the smaller mechanically evoked signals that characterize Emx2-positive hair cells.
source: In contrast, gpr156 zebrafish mutants lack the smaller mechanically evoked signals that characterize Emx2-positive hair cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 5.

claim: Loss of GPR156 does not affect orientation-selectivity of afferents in mouse utricle.
source: Loss of GPR156 does not affect orientation-selectivity of afferents in mouse utricle or zebrafish neuromasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by afferent labeling data in Figures 6-7.

claim: Loss of GPR156 does not affect orientation-selectivity of afferents in zebrafish neuromasts.
source: Loss of GPR156 does not affect orientation-selectivity of afferents in mouse utricle or zebrafish neuromasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single afferent labeling data in Figures 9-10.

claim: Gpr156 mutant mice do not show overt vestibular dysfunction.
source: Consistent with normal otolith organ anatomy and afferent selectivity, Gpr156 mutant mice do not show overt vestibular dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figures 11-12 showing normal balance beam performance and VOR responses.

claim: Performance on swimming tests is significantly altered in Gpr156 mutant mice.
source: Instead, performance on two tests that engage otolith organs is significantly altered – swimming and off-vertical-axis rotation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by swimming test data in Figure 11B.

claim: Performance on off-vertical-axis rotation is significantly altered in Gpr156 mutant mice.
source: Instead, performance on two tests that engage otolith organs is significantly altered – swimming and off-vertical-axis rotation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by OVAR data in Figure 12G-H.

claim: GPR156 relays hair cell orientation information downstream of EMX2.
source: We conclude that GPR156 relays hair cell orientation and transduction information downstream of EMX2, but not selectivity for direction-specific afferents.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings from mouse and zebrafish experiments.

claim: GPR156 relays transduction information downstream of EMX2.
source: We conclude that GPR156 relays hair cell orientation and transduction information downstream of EMX2, but not selectivity for direction-specific afferents.
evidence: This is based on zebrafish mechanosensitive data in Figure 5.

claim: GPR156 does not relay selectivity for direction-specific afferents downstream of EMX2.
source: We conclude that GPR156 relays hair cell orientation and transduction information downstream of EMX2, but not selectivity for direction-specific afferents.
evidence: This is based on afferent innervation data showing normal selectivity in Gpr156 mutants (Figures 6-10).

claim: Hair cells in otolith organs are oriented to respond to a range of head positions and linear motions in an approximately horizontal plane in the utricle.
source: In contrast, HCs in otolith organs are oriented to respond to a range of head positions and linear motions in an approximately horizontal (utricle) or vertical (saccule) plane (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Hair cells in otolith organs are oriented to respond to a range of head positions and linear motions in an approximately vertical plane in the saccule.
source: In contrast, HCs in otolith organs are oriented to respond to a range of head positions and linear motions in an approximately horizontal (utricle) or vertical (saccule) plane (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Hair cells show two opposing orientations across a virtual 'line of polarity reversal' (LPR) in otolith organs.
source: Within these planes, HCs show two opposing orientations across a virtual 'line of polarity reversal' (LPR), a conserved anatomical feature in all otolith organs (Denman-Johnson and Forge, 1999; Flock, 1964; Lindeman, 1969).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The LPR is a conserved anatomical feature in all otolith organs.
source: Within these planes, HCs show two opposing orientations across a virtual 'line of polarity reversal' (LPR), a conserved anatomical feature in all otolith organs (Denman-Johnson and Forge, 1999; Flock, 1964; Lindeman, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic anatomical studies.

claim: Striolar surface area is unchanged in Gpr156del/del mutant utricles compared to controls.
source: Graphs report striolar surface area and striolar HC density based on OCM labeling and show no change in mutants compared to heterozygote littermate controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with quantification and statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test).

claim: Striolar HC density is unchanged in Gpr156del/del mutant utricles compared to controls.
source: Graphs report striolar surface area and striolar HC density based on OCM labeling and show no change in mutants compared to heterozygote littermate controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with quantification and statistical analysis.

claim: Striolar surface area is unchanged in Gpr156del/del mutant saccules compared to controls.
source: Graphs report striolar surface area and striolar HC density based on OCM labeling and show no change in mutants compared to heterozygote littermate controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with quantification and statistical analysis.

claim: Striolar HC density is unchanged in Gpr156del/del mutant saccules compared to controls.
source: Graphs report striolar surface area and striolar HC density based on OCM labeling and show no change in mutants compared to heterozygote littermate controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with quantification and statistical analysis.

claim: Type I HC numbers are unchanged in all zones of Gpr156del/del mutant utricles and saccules compared to controls.
source: We observed no difference in SPP1-positive type I HC numbers between mutants and controls in any zone or organ (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with quantification using SPP1 labeling and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: Type II HC numbers are unchanged in all zones of Gpr156del/del mutant utricles and saccules compared to controls.
source: Again, we observed no difference in type II HC numbers between mutants and controls (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I with quantification using SOX2 labeling and two-way ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of GPR156 prevents Emx2-positive HCs from reversing their orientation but does not affect macular patterning.
source: In summary, loss of GPR156 prevents Emx2-positive HCs from reversing their orientation but does not affect macular patterning, including division into clear zones and appropriate numbers of type I and type II HCs throughout.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the anatomical data in Figure 1.

claim: Approximately 70% of LES HCs responded with detectable MET current to hair bundle deflection, regardless of HC type and genotype.
source: ~70% (93/135) of LES HCs responded with detectable IMET (within 20 pA) to hair bundle deflection, regardless of HC type and genotype (Chi-squared test, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings with statistical analysis (Chi-squared test).

claim: No significant differences were detected between genotypes for any Boltzmann parameter (Gmax, X1/2, or dx) in LES HCs.
source: Among the LES HCs tested, no significant differences were detected between genotypes for any Boltzmann parameter (Gmax, X1/2, or dx) (Figure 2F–G, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of G(X) curves from MET recordings shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: The operating range of MET was estimated to be approximately 800-900 nm for all LES HCs.
source: From G(X) relations, we estimated the operating range (OR; displacement range yielding 10–90% growth of GMET) to be ~800–900 nm for all LES HCs (Supp. File 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the G(X) data in Figure 2.

claim: No significant differences with genotype were detected in adaptation rates or extent in the LES.
source: In the LES, we detected no significant differences with genotype in adaptation rates or extent (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of adaptation kinetics from MET recordings.

claim: Type I HCs have many more K channels that are open around resting potential compared to type II HCs.
source: For example, type I HCs make relatively fast, small receptor potentials compared to type II HCs because type I HCs have many more K channels that are open around resting potential.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HC physiology.

claim: No effect of genotype was detected on the differences between type I and II HCs of the LES.
source: Again, no effect of genotype was detected on the differences between type I and II HCs of the LES (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on voltage-clamp recordings of K+ currents shown in Figure 3.

claim: Gpr156 is transcribed in all HCs across the maculae.
source: Loss of GPR156 does not impact HC orientation in the striola and MES, but Gpr156 is transcribed in all HCs across the maculae (Kindt et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kindt et al., 2021).

claim: No striking systematic differences with genotype were observed in voltage-gated or mechanotransduction currents from control vs. Gpr156 mutants in striola and MES zones.
source: While there was heterogeneity across HCs, we saw no striking systematic differences with genotype in the voltage-gated or mechanotransduction currents from control vs. Gpr156 mutants (but note that the statistical power of the comparisons is low, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each neuromast within the posterior lateral-line system of zebrafish has two populations of HCs that enable the detection of anterior- or posterior-directed fluid flow.
source: Similar to otolith organs of mammals, each neuromast within the posterior lateral-line system of zebrafish has two populations of HCs that enable the detection of anterior- or posterior-directed fluid flow (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish lateral line illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Both Emx2 and Gpr156 are required to reverse the orientation of one HC population in zebrafish neuromasts so that it can detect posterior flow.
source: To allow bi-directional detection, both Emx2 and Gpr156 are required to reverse the orientation of one HC population so that it can detect posterior flow (Figure 5A; Jiang et al., 2017; Kindt et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: In wild-type zebrafish, the mechanosensitive properties of HCs that detect anterior flow (Emx2-) are larger compared to those that detect posterior flow (Emx2+).
source: Previous work has shown that in wild-type animals, the mechanosensitive properties of HCs that detect anterior flow (Emx2-) are larger compared to those that detect posterior flow (Emx2+; Kindig et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kindig et al., 2023.

claim: Loss or gain of Emx2 in all lateral-line HCs was able to alter HC orientation and increase and decrease mechanosensitive responses, respectively.
source: Further, this work demonstrated that loss or gain of Emx2 in all lateral-line HCs was able to not only alter HC orientation, but also increase and decrease mechanosensitive responses, respectively (Kindig et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kindig et al., 2023.

claim: The magnitude of the mechanosensitive responses in gpr156 mutants was comparable to that of control P to A HCs.
source: Importantly, we found that the magnitude of the mechanosensitive responses in gpr156 mutants was comparable to that of control P to A HCs (e.g., Figure 5C and Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mechanosensitive responses were significantly larger in gpr156 mutants than control A to P HCs.
source: Further, the mechanosensitive responses were significantly larger in gpr156 mutants than control A to P HCs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on calcium imaging data with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.0043) shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The EMX2-GPR156 mechanism driving HC orientation reversal also affects the mechanosensitive properties of HCs in zebrafish neuromasts.
source: Together, this data suggests that the EMX2-GPR156 mechanism driving HC orientation reversal also affects the mechanosensitive properties of HCs in zebrafish neuromasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the calcium imaging data in Figure 5.

claim: Emx2 expression in the LES of the mouse utricle is required for afferents to innervate HCs of similar (rather than opposing) orientation.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that Emx2 expression in the LES of the mouse utricle and in HCs that sense posterior flow in the lateral line is required for afferents to innervate HCs of similar (rather than opposing) orientation (Ji et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ji et al., 2022 and Ji et al., 2018.

claim: All LES calyces belong to dimorphic afferents, which form both calyces on type I HCs and boutons on type II HCs.
source: All LES calyces belong to dimorphic afferents, which form both calyces on type I HCs and boutons on type II HCs.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations from dye-filling experiments.

claim: Terminal arbors in Gpr156del/+ control utricles comprised 1 or 2 calyces and as many as 65 boutons (median: 29).
source: Using this approach, we found that terminal arbors (receptive fields) in Gpr156del/+ control utricles (n=12) comprised 1 or 2 calyces and as many as 65 boutons (median: 29; Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is based on dye-filling data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Gpr156del/del utricles, labeled LES afferents were all dimorphic, terminating in up to three calyces and 56 boutons (median: 23).
source: In Gpr156del/del utricles, the labeled LES afferents (n=8) were also all dimorphic, terminating in up to three calyces and 56 boutons (median: 23).
evidence: This is based on dye-filling data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: The labeled receptive fields in Gpr156del/del utricles did not cross the striola/LES border.
source: The labeled receptive fields did not cross the striola/LES border (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is based on dye-filling data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: Advillin expression defines a population of neurons whose peripheral processes closely segregate with HC orientation, irrespective of striolar or extrastriolar HC identity.
source: This demonstrated that Advillin expression defines a population of neurons whose peripheral processes closely segregate with HC orientation, irrespective of striolar (OCM+) or extrastriolar (OCM-) HC identity.
evidence: This is based on Advillin-Cre genetic labeling data shown in Figure 7.

claim: HC innervation by Advillin-positive neurons was unchanged in Gpr156del/del mutants.
source: Importantly, HC innervation by Advillin-positive neurons was unchanged in Gpr156del/del mutants (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is based on Advillin-Cre labeling data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Equivalent numbers of OCM+ HCs were innervated in the lateral striola in Gpr156del/del mutants compared to controls.
source: We observed equivalent numbers of OCM+ HCs innervated in the lateral striola in Gpr156del/del mutants compared to controls (Mann-Whitney p=0.74; average OCM+/EGFP+ HCs per utricle: Gpr156del/+: 20.25, Gpr156del/del: 19.25; three animals and four utricles per genotype; no OCM+/EGFP+ HCs oriented towards the lateral edge were recorded in either genotype).
evidence: This is based on quantification of Advillin-Cre labeled neurons with statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test).

claim: The tendency of afferents to innervate HCs on one side of the LPR is not controlled by GPR156 or HC orientation.
source: In summary, we detected no anomaly in afferent receptive fields in utricles lacking GPR156 and thus lacking a LPR, showing that the tendency of afferents to innervate HCs on one side of the LPR is not controlled by GPR156 or HC orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the afferent labeling data in Figures 6-7.

claim: Striolar afferents have highly irregular inter-spike intervals, while extrastriolar afferents in both LES and MES have much more regular inter-spike intervals.
source: Striolar afferents have highly irregular inter-spike intervals, while extrastriolar afferents in both LES and MES have much more regular inter-spike intervals (Goldberg, 1991; Goldberg, 2000; Goldberg et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Goldberg's work.

claim: No difference was observed across genotypes in current threshold for spiking (Ithresh) in LES afferents.
source: No difference was observed across genotypes (Supplementary file 5): in both Gpr156del/+ afferents (n=18) and Gpr156del/del afferents (n=20), mean Ithresh was ~100 pA and ~95% of afferents produced sustained spiking at 3×Ithresh.
evidence: This is based on current-clamp recordings from afferents shown in Figure 8.

claim: Afferent firing patterns are unaltered in the LES of Gpr156del/del utricles, despite abnormal HC orientation.
source: These results suggest that afferent firing patterns, and likely the underlying ion channel expression, are unaltered in the LES of Gpr156del/del utricles, despite abnormal HC orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the afferent excitability data in Figure 8.

claim: Gpr156 mutant mice demonstrated impaired performance during swimming, characterized by underwater tumbling and the inability to maintain normal upright posture in the water.
source: However, when Gpr156del/del mice were placed in water, they demonstrated severely impaired swimming compared to Gpr156del/+ controls. This impairment was characterized by underwater tumbling and the inability to maintain normal upright posture in the water.
evidence: This is a primary behavioral finding supported by data in Figure 11B.

claim: The average time of rescue during swimming was significantly lower in Gpr156del/del compared to control mice.
source: All mice were rescued within 60 s and the average time of rescue was significantly lower in Gpr156del/del compared to control mice (Figure 11B; Gpr156del/+ controls = 49.9±3.0s; Gpr156del/del = 17.4±2.7s; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical analysis shown in Figure 11B.

claim: GPR156 is required for vestibular function important for swimming behavior.
source: Overall, these results indicated that GPR156 is required for vestibular function important for swimming behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the swimming test data.

claim: Both control and Gpr156del/del mice displayed robust compensatory eye movements during VORd, which increased as a function of frequency.
source: During VORd, both control and Gpr156del/del mice displayed robust compensatory eye movements, which increased as a function of frequency (Figure 12A–B).
evidence: This is based on VOR testing data shown in Figure 12A-B.

claim: The OKR responses of Gpr156del/del and control mice were comparable, confirming that there was no visual deficit in Gpr156 mutants.
source: The OKR responses of Gpr156del/del and control mice were comparable, confirming that there was no visual deficit in Gpr156 mutants (Figure 12C–D).
evidence: This is based on OKR testing data shown in Figure 12C-D.

claim: No difference was found in the VORl response of Gpr156del/del versus control mice.
source: Again, we found no difference in the VORl response of Gpr156del/del versus control mice in this lit environment (Figure 12E–F).
evidence: This is based on VOR in light testing data shown in Figure 12E-F.

claim: Gpr156del/del and control mice demonstrated a comparable percent change of gain decrease at each testing frequency during VOR motor learning.
source: Overall, Gpr156del/del and control mice demonstrated a comparable percent change of gain decrease at each testing frequencies (Figure 12—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on VOR adaptation testing data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Gpr156del/del and control mice demonstrated normal semicircular canals-driven responses.
source: Together, our VOR and OKR results indicated normal semicircular canals-driven responses in Gpr156del/del mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the VOR and OKR data in Figure 12A-F.

claim: Transient OVAR responses did not differ between control and Gpr156del/del mice.
source: Overall, our analysis revealed that transient OVAR responses did not differ between control and Gpr156del/del mice, supporting the proposal that absence of GPR156 did not affect canal-related ocular responses.
evidence: This is based on OVAR testing data shown in Figure 12G.

claim: Steady-state OVAR responses demonstrated a significantly impaired bias in Gpr156del/del mice as compared to controls.
source: In contrast, steady-state OVAR responses demonstrated a significantly impaired bias in Gpr156del/del mice as compared to controls (Figure 12G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on OVAR testing with statistical analysis shown in Figure 12G-H.

claim: The OVAR of Gpr156del/del mice was characterized by a significantly reduced bias relative to controls (Gpr156del/del: bias = 0.039 ± 0.26 versus control: bias = 3.85 ± 0.54, p=4.03E-5).
source: The OVAR of Gpr156del/del mice was characterized by a significantly reduced bias relative to controls (Gpr156del/del: bias = 0.039 ± 0.26 versus control: bias = 3.85 ± 0.54, p=4.03E-5).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical analysis from OVAR testing.

claim: The absence of HC reversal in Gpr156del/del alters otolith-mediated OVAR responses.
source: Thus taken together, these results show that the absence of HC reversal in Gpr156del/del alters otolith-mediated OVAR responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the OVAR data in Figure 12G-H.

claim: In mouse vestibular epithelia, HC orientation is controlled separately from other zonally differentiated properties of either HCs or afferents.
source: Taken together, our observations in utricles lacking GPR156 agree with other evidence that in mouse vestibular epithelia, HC orientation is controlled separately from other zonally differentiated properties of either HCs or afferents.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings from the study.

claim: Zebrafish lateral-line HCs use a combination of 2 mechanosensitive channels, Tmc2a and Tmc2b.
source: Zebrafish lateral-line HCs use a combination of 2 mechanosensitive channels, Tmc2a and Tmc2b (Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chou et al., 2017.

claim: In the posterior lateral line, Emx2+ HCs that sense posterior flow rely primarily on Tmc2b, while Emx2- HCs that sense anterior flow rely on both Tmc2a and Tmc2b.
source: In the posterior lateral line, Emx2+ HCs that sense posterior flow rely on primarily on Tmc2b, while Emx2- HCs that sense anterior flow rely on both Tmc2a and Tmc2b.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish lateral line mechanotransduction.

claim: Emx2+ HCs that rely primarily on Tmc2b have smaller mechanosensitive responses compared to Emx2- HCs that rely on both Tmc2a and Tmc2b.
source: Recently, a functional asymmetry was discovered between anterior- and posterior-sensitive HCs: Emx2+ HCs that rely primarily on Tmc2b have smaller mechanosensitive responses compared to Emx2- HCs that rely on both Tmc2a and Tmc2b (Kindig et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kindig et al., 2023.

claim: Functional asymmetry was lost in gpr156 mutants.
source: In our present study we find that functional asymmetry was also lost in gpr156 mutants (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on calcium imaging data in Figure 5.

claim: Zebrafish Emx2 may act through Gpr156 to impact Tmc2a/2b function.
source: As the Gpr156 receptor is unlikely to act transcriptionally, zebrafish Emx2 may act through Gpr156 to impact Tmc2a/2b function.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings.

claim: Both Emx2 and Gpr156 are important to dictate HC orientation and the mechanosensitive properties of HCs with opposing orientations.
source: Overall, our work in zebrafish indicates that both Emx2 and Gpr156 are important to dictate HC orientation and the mechanosensitive properties of HCs with opposing orientations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the zebrafish data in Figure 5.

claim: Current results are consistent with normal HC function in the Gpr156 mouse mutant.
source: Nevertheless, current results are consistent with normal HC function in the Gpr156 mouse mutant, a prerequisite to interrogate how non-reversed HCs affects vestibular behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data in Figures 2-4.

claim: In mammals, only otolith organs (utricle, saccule) have a LPR.
source: In mammals, only otolith organs (utricle, saccule) have a LPR.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The absence of a LPR in Gpr156 mutants should only affect otolith-driven reflexes and behaviors.
source: Therefore, the absence of a LPR in Gpr156 mutants should only affect otolith-driven reflexes and behaviors.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Visual and quantitative assessments did not reveal circling or head tremor behaviors in Gpr156del/del mice at rest.
source: Visual and quantitative assessments did not reveal circling or head tremor behaviors in Gpr156del/del mice at rest (Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both control and Gpr156del/del mice scored 0 (normal) on tail hanging, air righting, and contact inhibition of righting behavioral tests.
source: Both control and Gpr156del/del mice scored 0 (where 0=normal, see Methods) on each of these behavioral tests (Figure 11—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both Gpr156del/del and Gpr156del/+ mice showed normal coordination on the balance beam.
source: On the balance beam, both Gpr156del/del and Gpr156del/+ mice showed normal coordination (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is based on balance beam testing data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Markedly impaired swimming performance could be due to deficits in the otolith rather than semicircular canal dependent pathways.
source: We hypothesized that markedly impaired swimming performance could be due to deficits in the otolith rather than semicircular canal dependent pathways.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the swimming deficit observations.

claim: Gpr156 does not appear to be significantly expressed in the central nervous system according to the Allen Brain Atlas.
source: Gpr156 does not appear to be significantly expressed in the central nervous system according to the Allen Brain Atlas (Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Allen Brain Atlas (Lein et al., 2007).

claim: Vestibular ganglion neurons still selectively innervated LES HCs even when lacking GPR156.
source: In addition, Advillin-Cre tracing and dye-filling experiments (Figures 6, 7) showed that vestibular ganglion neurons still selectively innervated LES HCs even when lacking GPR156.
evidence: This is based on the afferent labeling data in Figures 6-7.

claim: HC signals in the LES zone of Gpr156 mutants are relayed to the cerebellum via the central projection of Advillin+ neurons as usual, but with abnormal (non-reversed) response polarity.
source: We thus speculate that HC signals in the LES zone of Gpr156 mutants are relayed to the cerebellum (Ji et al., 2022; Maklad et al., 2010) via the central projection of Advillin+ neurons as usual, but with abnormal (non-reversed) response polarity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings and citations.

claim: It appears unlikely that vestibular deficits observed in constitutive Gpr156 mouse mutants reflect defective neuronal activity in addition to a missing LPR.
source: Overall, it appears unlikely that vestibular deficits observed in our constitutive Gpr156 mouse mutants reflect defective neuronal activity in addition to a missing LPR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings.

claim: Vestibular deficits in Gpr156 and Emx2 mouse models are relatively mild (normal balance beam, VOR and OKR).
source: Regarding behavior, this study and work by Ji et al., 2022 agree that vestibular deficits in each model are relatively mild (normal balance beam, VOR and OKR).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work (Ji et al., 2022).

claim: Emx2 inactivation in HCs (Gfi1-Cre) showed impaired swimming ability, but defects were less severe and different in nature compared to constitutive Gpr156 mutants.
source: Emx2 inactivation in HCs (Gfi1-Cre) showed impaired swimming ability, but defects were less severe and different in nature compared to constitutive Gpr156 mutants.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work (Ji et al., 2022).

claim: Gpr156 mutants displayed substantial difficulty in maintaining their orientation in water, and frequently rolled over such that they needed to be rescued.
source: Gpr156 mutants displayed substantial difficulty in maintaining their orientation in water, and frequently rolled over such that they needed to be rescued.
evidence: This is based on swimming test observations.

claim: Emx2 mutants did not need rescue during swimming and were described as demonstrating 'frantic' swimming behavior, spending more time trying to climb out of the water as compared to their littermate controls.
source: In contrast, Emx2 mutants did not need rescue and were described as demonstrating 'frantic' swimming behavior, spending more time trying to climb out of the water as compared to their littermate controls.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work (Ji et al., 2022).

claim: GPR156 acts downstream of EMX2 to regulate hair bundle orientation.
source: GPR156 acts downstream of EMX2 to regulate hair bundle orientation, and perhaps mechanosensitivity in zebrafish.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings from the study.

claim: Afferent projections segregate with HC orientation and not with zonal identity.
source: Another significant new result in the current study is to show that afferent projections segregate with HC orientation and not with zonal identity (Figure 7; Advillin neuron labeling), yet segregation does not depend on HC orientation since it is unchanged in mouse and zebrafish Gpr156 mutants (Figures 6—10).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on data in Figures 6-10.
